title: Co‐evaluation of co‐production in mind and brain research: A dialogical approach
abstract: Abstract Co‐production is increasingly used in mental and neurological health research, but less is known about how co‐production itself can be co‐evaluated. We conducted a study that aimed to systematically co‐evaluate a 9‐month project that co‐produced strategic priorities and internal research‐funding procedures for a new mind and brain research centre. The co‐evaluation used a mixed‐method design, including qualitative, quantitative, dialogical and post‐implementation approaches, informed by an adapted RQ + 4 Co‐Pro framework. The project involved 14 adult contributors who were also participants in the co‐evaluation, including seven community partners alongside academic, clinical and research staff. Contributors across these roles also brought lived or living experience of mental‐health difficulties, neurodivergence and marginalisation. Reflexive thematic analysis examined contributors' written reflections; perceived power was measured midway through the project and again at completion; findings were returned to the team for dialogical co‐interpretation; and funding‐panel members later reflected on implementation of the co‐produced procedures. Thematic analysis generated six themes concerning time and resources, roles and identities, leadership and power, communication, institutional barriers and emotional labour and gains. Mean Sense of Power scores increased from 5.34 to 5.61 ( p = .023). Dialogical reflection revealed both convergent and differing interpretations of shared experiences. Our central learning was that equitable co‐production requires time to build trust, enough structure for collective work to progress without closing down shared influence and institutional systems able to support participation. By retaining rather than resolving different viewpoints, we show how systematic, dialogical co‐evaluation can turn contrasting experiences into practical learning for future co‐production.
